582.title: Unmoved by pain
582.hook: jo nar dukh mai dukh nahee maanai: the one unmoved by pain, pleasure, praise, gold or dust (Sorath M9, ang 633)
582.howItsDone: Guru Tegh Bahadur's Sorath shabad 'jo nar dukh mai dukh nahee maanai' is sung in kirtan, and Sikhs often recall its portrait of steadiness in times of grief or illness.

segments.voice: Yesterday, rachnaa: the creation, passing like a dream. If the world is passing, how do you stand in it? Today's hymn answers.

Stub your toe on the bed frame at night, and there are two pains. The first is the toe: sharp, real, over in a minute. The second arrives a moment later. Why is the bed there? Why does this always happen to me? Everything's ruined. The second pain can last for hours, and it's mostly made of words. A hymn of Guru Tegh Bahadur's in Raag Sorath begins with someone who feels the first pain, and doesn't add the second.
screen: `THE STUBBED TOE: THE FIRST PAIN.` → `THE STORY: THE SECOND PAIN.` → `FEELING ONE, NOT ADDING TWO.`

segments.voice: The hymn opens jo nar dukh mai dukh nahee maanai. The one who, in pain, doesn't take pain as pain. Dukh is pain, sorrow. Maanai is to accept, to take something as so. The line doesn't say this person feels nothing. It says that in the middle of dukh, they don't crown it king. Then the hymn draws a portrait, in paraphrase. No clinging to pleasure, no fear. Gold and dust seen alike. No slander, no flattery, no greed, attachment or pride. Apart from joy and grief, from honor and dishonor. Hopes and cravings set down. Lust and anger can't touch this person, and in that heart, the hymn says, God lives. Who can live like this? Only the one the Guru has blessed, it says, understands the way. And the last line is a picture: Nanak has merged with the Lord, like water with water. Pour water into water, and there's no seam, nothing to defend. That's the inner reason for the steadiness. The one who is level in all weather isn't gritting their teeth. They've stopped holding themselves apart. And this isn't coldness. Sikh teaching calls for service, sharing and standing up for others, and Sikhs remember the ninth Guru as giving his life to defend other people's freedom of faith. This steadiness is the calm that lets you act well in a storm, instead of being thrown around by it.

segments.voice: Check in with whatever mood is here, restless, low, cheerful, tired, and feel it the way you'd feel weather on your face, without changing it. When the story about the mood starts, I shouldn't feel this, this will last forever, come back to the breath and let the mood pass over a steady field. If you pray, you can rest in Waheguru between breaths.
Dukh, pain or sorrow. In Guru Tegh Bahadur's Sorath hymn, the one who doesn't take it as pain is level through every weather, merged with the Lord like water with water.
Your line: level in all weather. The first pain is real; the second is mostly words. More tomorrow.

583.title: Friends in good times
583.hook: everyone is a companion in pleasure; in trouble, few remain (Sorath M9, ang 634)
583.howItsDone: When a Sikh family loses someone, the sangat often gathers at the home with food and support while a reading of the Guru Granth Sahib is held, and Guru Tegh Bahadur's hymns and saloks are commonly heard at that time.

segments.voice: Yesterday, dukh: feel the first pain, don't add the second, and stay level in all weather. Today the ninth Guru looks at the people around us when the weather turns.

When someone gets a promotion, the group chat lights up. Congratulations, drinks on you, so proud of you, a row of party emojis. When the same person loses the job six months later, the chat goes quiet. A couple of people send a private message. Most say nothing, not out of cruelty, but because they don't know what to say, and it's easier to look away. Guru Tegh Bahadur saw it too, long before group chats, and put it in a hymn.
screen: `A PROMOTION: THE CHAT LIGHTS UP.` → `A LOSS: THE CHAT GOES QUIET.` → `HE SAW IT TOO.`

segments.voice: The hymn in Raag Sorath begins, in paraphrase: friend, understand this in your mind. The world is bound up in its own comfort; no one truly belongs to anyone. In good times, many come and sit with you, crowding round on every side. When trouble falls, they all leave your company, and no one comes near. Sukh is comfort, good times. Bipat is trouble, calamity. The hymn's line runs between those two words. Then it goes further than most of us would dare. Even the one at home who loved you most, it says, when the soul leaves the body, runs away crying ghost. It's a hard sentence, and it's meant to be. The point isn't that people are wicked. It's that human love, left to itself, is tangled up with what we get from each other. The hymn ends: at the last, says Nanak, nothing helps except the Lord. Yet it doesn't tell you to become bitter. If everyone drifts off when trouble comes, the one who stays is rare, and Sikh tradition prizes that rarity. Look at the sangat that turns up with food when someone dies, sitting with the family for days while the Guru Granth Sahib is read. That's a whole community built to stay. The hymn describes how the world tends to drift away. The practice asks you to be the exception.
screen: `NO ONE TRULY BELONGS TO ANYONE.` · `SUKH: MANY COME AND SIT.` · `BIPAT: NO ONE COMES NEAR.` · `BE THE ONE WHO STAYS.` · then, large: `STAY IN HARD TIMES.`

segments.voice: Let one name come to mind, someone going through something hard right now, an illness, a breakup, a lost job, a long grief, and notice if part of you has been keeping away, not sure what to say. Choose one way to come near, a message, a visit, a meal left at the door, a call where you mostly listen; you don't need wise words, only to show up. If you pray, you can hold them before Waheguru.
Preet, love. Guru Tegh Bahadur's Sorath hymn looks honestly at how much of our love is tied to our own comfort: many sit with us in sukh, good times, and few come near in bipat, trouble.
Your line: stay in hard times. Two lines in a message can be enough. Five hundred eighty-three days now.

584.title: Why search in the forest
584.hook: kaahe re ban khojan jaaee: why look in the forest; He is within, like scent in a flower (Dhanasri M9, ang 684)
584.howItsDone: Guru Tegh Bahadur's Dhanasri shabad 'kaahe re ban khojan jaaee' is sung in kirtan; Sikhs often cite its images of the flower's scent and the mirror's reflection for the teaching that God is found within ordinary life.

segments.voice: Yesterday, preet: many sit with you in good times, and the one who stays in hard times is rare. Today, where the One who stays can be found.

You're late, and you can't find your glasses. Kitchen counter, coat pocket, under the sofa cushions, the car. You ask everyone in the house. Ten minutes of rising panic. Then you catch yourself in the hallway mirror, and there they are, pushed up on top of your head. The thing you were hunting for was with you the whole time. Guru Tegh Bahadur's hymn in Raag Dhanasri begins with a gentle question for a seeker setting out for the forest, to look for God far from ordinary life.
screen: `THE GLASSES ON YOUR HEAD.` → `SEEKERS WHO LEFT FOR THE FOREST.` → `A GENTLE QUESTION.`

segments.voice: The hymn opens kaahe re ban khojan jaaee. Why go searching in the forest? Ban is forest; khojan is to search. Then, in paraphrase: the One who dwells in everything, and is always untouched, is with you, absorbed in you. And two pictures. As fragrance lives inside a flower, and as a reflection lives inside a mirror, so the Lord lives within, without a break. Search within your own heart, brother. You can't see a flower's scent, or pull it out and hold it. But it's in every petal, and the moment you lean close, it's there. And the face in the mirror isn't somewhere else, waiting to be found. It appears exactly where you're looking. Then the hymn adds, in paraphrase: know the One as the same, outside and inside; this is the wisdom the Guru has taught. So it isn't saying God is only inside and the world is empty. Inside and outside are one presence. And the last line: says Nanak, without knowing your own self, the moss of doubt is not cleared away. Kaaee is the green moss that grows on still water and hides it. Sikh teaching keeps the search inside ordinary life, the householder's life of work and family. The hymn doesn't condemn the forest. It just says the One is already here, like the scent in the flower you're holding.
screen: `BAN: WHY SEARCH THE FOREST?` · `SCENT IN THE FLOWER.` · `A FACE IN THE MIRROR.` · `CLEAR THE MOSS OF DOUBT.` · then, large: `SCENT IN THE FLOWER.`

segments.voice: Bring something fragrant close, a flower, a herb, a piece of fruit, a cup of tea, and breathe in slowly, noticing that the scent is invisible and everywhere in it; if nothing's near, remember a smell you love, rain on dust, bread, a rose. Then sit with the hymn's idea that what you're looking for may be this close. If you pray, you can rest in Waheguru between breaths.
Baas, fragrance. Guru Tegh Bahadur's Dhanasri hymn says the Lord lives within, like baas in a flower and a face in a mirror.
Your line: scent in the flower. Peace isn't only after the trip or the move; it can be right where you are. Until tomorrow.

585.title: Remember, remember
585.hook: raam simar raam simar ihai tero kaaj hai: remember, this is your real work (Jaijavanti M9, ang 1352)
585.howItsDone: Many Sikhs begin the day with simran, repeating Waheguru, before Nitnem and the day's work; Guru Tegh Bahadur's Jaijavanti shabad 'raam simar raam simar' is sung in kirtan as a call to that practice.

segments.voice: Yesterday, baas: the Lord lives within, like scent in a flower. If the One is that close, what do you do about it? Today's hymn gives a job.

A to-do list on a Monday morning. Reply to the landlord. Book the dentist. Finish the report. Buy milk. Call Mom back. Return the package. It's long, and everything on it feels urgent. Now imagine someone gently taking the pen and writing one more line at the very top, above all of it, underlined twice. Not instead of the list. Above it. Guru Tegh Bahadur's hymn in Raag Jaijavanti does exactly that. It opens with a word said twice, and then says what your real work is.
screen: `A MONDAY TO-DO LIST.` → `ONE LINE WRITTEN AT THE TOP.` → `A WORD SAID TWICE.`

segments.voice: The hymn opens raam simar, raam simar, ihai tero kaaj hai. Remember the Lord, remember the Lord: this is your work. Simar is the root of simran: remembering, keeping the Lord in mind, often by repeating the Name. Raam, in Gurbani, is the all-pervading One. And kaaj is work, the job you came to do. Why say it twice? Think of how you call someone who's drifting off: hey, hey. The doubling is a hand on the shoulder. Then, in paraphrase: leave the company of maya, and take shelter with the Lord. Know the world's pleasures to be false; all this show is passing. Know wealth as a dream; why be proud of it? The kingdom of the whole earth is like a wall of sand. And near the end, Nanak says the body will perish, as time slips away moment by moment. Here's the surprise. The hymn doesn't call remembering a hobby, or a reward for when the work is done. It calls it the work. Sikhs hear the same thought in a hymn of Guru Arjan's in the evening prayer: no other task will help you; join the holy company and meditate on the Name alone. So the list doesn't vanish. You still buy the milk and call your mother. But the line at the top changes the rest, because the other jobs no longer carry your whole worth. That's simran: the work under all the work.

segments.voice: Before the list, the phone or the inbox, sit and breathe slowly. If you pray, repeat Waheguru quietly, once on each breath, the way Sikhs practice simran; if you don't, come back again and again to the plain fact that you're here and alive. When the list starts calling, let it wait.
Remember. Raam simar, raam simar: Guru Tegh Bahadur says twice that remembering the Lord is your real work, the job under every other job.
Your line: this is your work. The list still gets done; it just isn't at the top. Day five hundred eighty-five, done.

586.title: It is passing
586.hook: beet jaihai: it is passing, life is passing in vain (Jaijavanti M9, ang 1352)
586.howItsDone: Guru Tegh Bahadur's Jaijavanti shabad 'beet jaihai beet jaihai' is sung in kirtan; Sikhs often hear its ticking refrain as a call to fill life with remembrance and devotion.

segments.voice: Yesterday, remember: remembering the Lord is your real work. Today's hymn, in the same raga, asks what happens when that work is left undone.

Forty minutes. That's how long the phone held on before you looked up. Not spent, exactly. Just gone. You can't say what you saw. You weren't resting and you weren't working. The time slipped through without leaving a mark. Now stretch that out. A month like that. A year. Guru Tegh Bahadur's next hymn in Raag Jaijavanti opens with two words, said twice, like a clock ticking: beet jaihai, beet jaihai.
screen: `FORTY MINUTES, GONE.` → `A MONTH, A YEAR.` → `BEET JAIHAI, BEET JAIHAI.`

segments.voice: The full line is beet jaihai, beet jaihai, janam akaaj re. It is passing, it is passing: life, without its work. Beet is to pass, to slip by. And akaaj links back to yesterday. Kaaj was your work; akaaj is without the work, idle, done for nothing. Yesterday's hymn said remembering is your kaaj. Today's says what life becomes without it. Then, in paraphrase: night and day you hear the scriptures recited, and still you don't understand, unknowing one. Death has already arrived; where will you run? The body you thought was permanent will turn to dust. Why don't you take the Lord's Name? The word for what's heard is puraan, the old sacred stories people listened to recited. But the fault isn't in the stories. It's hearing holy words without letting them in, and that can happen to anyone, including someone who hears Gurbani every morning and lets it slide past like background music. Then the hymn turns. In paraphrase: bring devotion to the Lord into your heart, and let go of the mind's pride. Says Nanak, this is the way to live in the world, shining. The word is biraaj, to dwell in splendor, like a king on a throne. So the hymn starts with a ticking clock and ends with a person living brightly. The passing is real; what fills it is up to us. Said slowly, the line isn't grim. It's a wake-up call: it is passing, so live it.

segments.voice: Look at the next few hours of your day and choose one, then decide what would make that hour not akaaj, not empty: work done with full attention, a walk with someone you love, real rest, or time with a shabad. Then let the plan go and simply breathe, feeling this minute pass, fully. If you pray, you can rest in Waheguru between breaths.

Your line: live in the world, shining. Biraaj: a life lit up, not just used up. That's today.

587.title: Fifteen ragas
587.hook: his shabads are spread across fifteen ragas, the last in Jaijavanti, found nowhere else in the Granth
587.howItsDone: Ragis in the gurdwara sing Guru Tegh Bahadur's shabads in the ragas the Granth sets them in, so the melody carries the mood the hymn was written for.

segments.voice: Yesterday, beet: life is passing, so live it, shining. Two days running, the hymns came from Raag Jaijavanti. Today, the music itself.

Some songs take you somewhere else the moment they start. A tune from a wedding, a lullaby a grandmother hummed, the radio in a hospital waiting room. Before any word arrives, the melody has already changed your mood. Musicians in India have long organized that power into ragas: frameworks of notes and movement, each with its own feeling, often its own season or hour. The Guru Granth Sahib is built on them. And one raga in it belongs, as far as the book is concerned, to a single Guru.
screen: `A TUNE THAT TAKES YOU SOMEWHERE.` → `RAGAS: NOTES WITH A FEELING.` → `ONE RAGA, ONE GURU.`

segments.voice: Most of the Guru Granth Sahib is arranged by raga. Past the opening prayers, you move through thirty-one raga sections: Sri, Majh, Gauri, Asa, and on. Inside each, the hymns are grouped by Guru, and each is meant to be sung in that raga's mood. Guru Tegh Bahadur's shabads, commonly counted at fifty-nine, are spread across fifteen of them: Gauri, Asa, Sorath, Dhanasri, Bilaval, Ramkali, Maru, Basant, Sarang, and others. You've already met him in Gauri, with pride and the passing creation; in Sorath, with the steady one and the friends who leave; and in Dhanasri, with the scent in the flower. Then there's Jaijavanti. It's the last raga section in the Granth's order, and it's tiny: four shabads. All four are his. No other Guru, and none of the saints whose hymns sit in the Granth, has a hymn in Jaijavanti. The sources don't say why he chose it, or why it appears nowhere else. Some musicians describe Jaijavanti as mixing two moods, a little longing alongside something bright. And those four shabads are the ones you've just heard, remember, remember, and it is passing, with two more like them. The compilers could have tucked his hymns into a nearby raga. Instead, the Granth gives the ninth Guru a short room of his own, near the end of the book. The quiet voice has a raga of his own.

588.title: Living his calm
588.hook: detachment here means love without clutching
588.howItsDone: The Sikh path is a householder's path, with work and family, and Sikhs describe the Gurus' ideal as staying unattached in the world like a lotus in water; Guru Tegh Bahadur's hymns are often sung as reminders of that steady, open love.

segments.voice: Yesterday, fifteen ragas, and Jaijavanti, a raga of his own. All week the ninth Guru has said the world is passing. Today, how to live it.
screen: `FIFTEEN RAGAS — A RAGA OF HIS OWN.`

segments.voice: A parent is teaching a child to ride a bike, running alongside with one hand on the back of the seat. At some point the hand has to come off, a little at a time. Grip too tight and the child never learns to balance. Let go too soon and they fall. The love is in the loosening. All week, Guru Tegh Bahadur has been saying the world is passing. So should we love it less?
screen: `RUNNING ALONGSIDE THE BIKE.` → `THE LOVE IS IN THE LOOSENING.` → `SHOULD WE LOVE LESS?`

segments.voice: In Sikh teaching, detachment doesn't mean running away. It's a householder's path. Guru Tegh Bahadur was married to Mata Gujri, and was father to the boy who became Guru Gobind Singh. Tradition remembers long years of quiet meditation at Bakala, and he still lived in a family, traveled, founded the town that became Anandpur, and in the end went to Delhi, where Sikhs remember he gave his life for others. So when his hymns say the world is passing, the point isn't to stop caring. Look at the week. The steady one in Sorath sees gold and dust alike, and merges with the Lord like water into water. The friends who leave in hard times were loving their own comfort. The scent is in the flower, not in the forest. Remembering is the real work, and life without it slips by. Put them together and you get a love that holds without gripping. Guru Nanak gave Sikhs the picture for it: a lotus that grows in water but stays dry, a duck that swims all day and isn't soaked. Those are the images Sikhs reach for when they talk about living in the world without drowning in it. Love without clutching isn't loving less. It's loving without needing to own. You can cherish your children and still let them become who they are. You can enjoy your home and not fall apart when the roof leaks. The calm in the ninth Guru's hymns isn't distance. It's the open hand that lets love stay.
screen: `DETACHMENT ISN'T RUNNING AWAY.` · `THE GURU WAS A HOUSEHOLDER.` · `THE LOTUS IN WATER STAYS DRY.` · `THE OPEN HAND LETS LOVE STAY.` · then, large: `LOVE WITHOUT CLUTCHING.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone you love deeply, and notice any place where love has turned into gripping: worry about their choices, a need for them to call, a fear of losing them. Without scolding yourself, open your hands in your lap, palms up, and hold them in mind the way that parent's hand rests on the bike seat, there but light, wishing them well exactly as they are. If you pray, you can place them in Waheguru's care.
Kamal, lotus. In Guru Tegh Bahadur's hymns, detachment means love without clutching: living in the world like a kamal in water.
Your line: love without clutching. Like a lotus: in the water, and not drowned by it. That's day five hundred eighty-eight.
